nuh.text:
Stories from the Quran · 1
Nuh and the Great Ark
نوح والسفينة

From the Quran
وَحَمَلْنَٰهُ عَلَىٰ ذَاتِ أَلْوَٰحٍ وَدُسُرٍ
And We carried him on a [construction of] planks and nails,
Al-Qamar 54:13 · Saheeh International

Long, long ago, people forgot Allah. They carved great stones with their own hands, gave them names, and bowed down to them.
So Allah sent them a prophet, a kind and patient man named Nuh (peace be upon him).
keep: Five tall stones. The Quran names five idols of Nuh’s people: Wadd, Suwa‘, Yaghuth, Ya‘uq and Nasr (71:23).

nuh.text:
“My people, worship Allah alone, and ask Him to forgive you,” Nuh told them. He called them by day, and he called them by night. He called them out loud, and he spoke to them quietly, one by one.
But they put their fingers in their ears and pulled their cloaks over their heads.
keep: Half day, half night. Nuh said, “I called my people night and day” (71:5).

nuh.text:
Nuh did not give up. He called his people for nine hundred and fifty years, so long that the stars turned in the sky night after night after night.
But only a few believed.
keep: There are 950 tiny stars in this sky, one for each year Nuh called his people (29:14).

nuh.text:
Then Allah told Nuh: “Build the ark, while We watch over you and guide you.”
So Nuh cut wood and shaped planks, one after another, long and strong.

He built the ark far from any sea. Every time the chiefs walked past, they laughed at him. “A ship on dry land!”
Nuh answered calmly: “You laugh at us now. Soon you will know.”
keep: Planks and nails. The Quran describes the ark as “planks and nails” (54:13). Count the nails on its side.

nuh.text:
Then the sign came that Allah had promised. Water came gushing up out of the oven, where no water should be!
It was time.
keep: The oven. In Hud 11:40 and Al-Mu’minun 23:27 the sign was water gushing from an oven, the tannūr.

nuh.text:
“Carry in the ark two of every kind,” said Allah, “a pair of each, with your family and those who believe.”
Up the ramp they went, two by two: big and small, fast and slow, furry and feathered.

“Climb in,” said Nuh. “In the name of Allah it sails, and in the name of Allah it comes to rest.”
The door was shut, and the first drops of rain began to fall.
Then the sky opened with pouring rain, and the earth burst open with springs. The water from above and the water from below met, just as Allah had planned.
keep: Water from above and water from below meeting (54:11–12).

nuh.text: The ark sailed on through waves as high as mountains. Inside, everyone was safe.

Nuh saw one of his sons standing apart. “My son, come with us!” he called. But his son said, “I will climb a mountain. It will keep me safe.”
“Nothing can keep anyone safe today except Allah’s mercy,” said Nuh. Then a wave came between them.

At last Allah said: “O earth, swallow your water! O sky, hold back your rain!”
The rain stopped. The water sank down into the earth. And it was all over.
The ark came to rest high on a mountain called Al-Judi. The sun came out, and the air smelled fresh and new.

“Go down in peace from Us,” Allah said to Nuh, “with blessings on you and on those with you.”
Out they came, two by two, into a washed and shining world.
Grass grew. Flowers opened. Birds sang again. The animals spread across the land, and the people who believed started their lives again.
Nuh thanked Allah and prayed: “My Lord, forgive me and my parents, and everyone who enters my house believing, and all believing men and women.”
Allah saved Nuh and those with him in the laden ship. And He made the ark a sign for all people, to remember forever.
keep: The little fish on the flag. “The laden ship” is how the Quran describes Nuh’s ark (26:119), and the very same words describe Yunus’s ship (37:140). Find it in book 6.

nuh.text:
Say Nuh’s words
Say them when you climb aboard a boat, a car or a plane.
بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِBismillāhIn the name of Allah

What does the story teach us?
Keep going.
Nuh called his people for 950 years and never gave up.

Did you know?
Nuh’s name appears 43 times in the Quran. A whole surah is named after him: Surah Nuh, number 71. Can you count the dots?
Every verse of the Quran is one tiny square, starting at the top right like a page of the Quran. Each dot is a verse that names Nuh.
He called his people for “a thousand years less fifty”: that is how the Quran says 950 (29:14).

Look closer
Some pictures hide a secret from the Quran itself. Go back and find them.
p. 3Five tall stones. The Quran names five idols of Nuh’s people: Wadd, Suwa‘, Yaghuth, Ya‘uq and Nasr (71:23).p. 4Half day, half night. Nuh said, “I called my people night and day” (71:5).p. 5There are 950 tiny stars in this sky, one for each year Nuh called his people (29:14).p. 7Planks and nails. The Quran describes the ark as “planks and nails” (54:13). Count the nails on its side.p. 8The oven. In Hud 11:40 and Al-Mu’minun 23:27 the sign was water gushing from an oven, the tannūr.p. 11Water from above and water from below meeting (54:11–12).p. 19The little fish on the flag. “The laden ship” is how the Quran describes Nuh’s ark (26:119), and the very same words describe Yunus’s ship (37:140). Find it in book 6.

For parents
Where the story is told. Hud 11:25–49, Al-Mu’minun 23:23–30, Ash-Shu‘ara 26:105–122, Al-Qamar 54:9–15, Nuh 71:1–28 and Al-‘Ankabut 29:14–15.
Told in simple words. This is a retelling for young children, not a translation. The events follow the verses listed. The pictures add ordinary scene-setting, such as the forest the wood came from. There is no rainbow: it belongs to the Bible’s telling, not the Quran’s.
The son. The Quran tells of Nuh’s son who would not board (11:42–43), and Nuh’s plea for him (11:45–46). It is told gently here; your child may want to talk about it.
The pictures. By custom, no prophet is drawn, and in this series no person at all. The pictures show the places, the light and the creatures, so your child can picture the story around them.
Talk about it. Nuh kept going for 950 years. What is something you find hard but keep trying?
Illustrators welcome. These first pictures are a starting point. Artists are invited to redraw any book; the Books page of the Quran Atlas has a brief for every page.

ibrahim.text:
Stories from the Quran · 2
Ibrahim and the Fire
إبراهيم والنار

From the Quran
قُلْنَا يَٰنَارُ كُونِى بَرْدًا وَسَلَٰمًا عَلَىٰٓ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ
Allah said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."
Al-Anbiyaʾ 21:69 · Saheeh International

Long ago, in a land between two great rivers, there lived a boy named Ibrahim (peace be upon him).
His father, Azar, carved statues out of wood and stone. People bought them, set them up, and bowed down to them.

Ibrahim looked at the statues. They could not see. They could not hear. They could not even brush away a fly.
“How can something we make with our own hands be our god?” he wondered.

One night Ibrahim saw a bright star shining. “Is this my Lord?” he asked.
But the star set and was gone. “I do not love things that disappear,” said Ibrahim.
keep: The star, the moon and the sun. The same three appear again in Yusuf’s dream (12:4). Find them in book 3.

ibrahim.text:
Then he saw the moon rising, big and silver. “Is this my Lord?”
But the moon set too. “If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be lost,” said Ibrahim.
keep: The star, the moon and the sun. The same three appear again in Yusuf’s dream (12:4). Find them in book 3.

ibrahim.text:
In the morning the sun rose, huge and golden. “This must be my Lord! This is the biggest of all!”
But in the evening the sun set as well.
keep: The star, the moon and the sun. The same three appear again in Yusuf’s dream (12:4). Find them in book 3.

ibrahim.text:
Then Ibrahim said: “I turn my face to the One who made the heavens and the earth.”
The star, the moon and the sun all come and go. Allah made them all, and Allah never disappears.

Ibrahim went to his people. “What are these statues you sit in front of all day?”
“We found our fathers worshipping them,” they said.
“Then you and your fathers have been clearly wrong,” said Ibrahim.

One day the people went out of the city for a festival, and the temple was empty. Ibrahim went in. Plates of food sat in front of the statues.
“Won’t you eat?” he asked them. “Why don’t you speak?”
Of course, they said nothing.
keep: Plates of food in front of the statues. Ibrahim asked them, “Won’t you eat?” (37:91).

ibrahim.text: So Ibrahim broke the statues into pieces, all of them except the biggest one.
keep: Only the biggest statue is left standing (21:58). The axe hanging on it comes from the old commentaries.

ibrahim.text:
When the people came back, they cried, “Who did this to our gods?”
“Ask them,” said Ibrahim, “if they can speak! Perhaps the biggest one did it.”
The people looked down. They knew statues cannot speak.

But instead of listening, they grew angry. “Burn him!” they shouted. “Protect your gods!”
They gathered wood, more and more, and built an enormous fire.
The fire roared so high and hot that no one could go near it. And they threw Ibrahim into the flames.

Then Allah said:
“O fire, be cool, and safe, for Ibrahim!”
And the fire obeyed.
keep: Blue flames. Allah said “cool” and then “safe” (21:69). Commentators said “safe” was added so the fire would not become harmfully cold.

ibrahim.text:
The fire did not hurt Ibrahim at all. He walked out safe and well.
The people had made a plan against him, but Allah made their plan fail.

Many years later, Ibrahim and his son Isma‘il were in a dry valley among bare mountains. Allah showed them where to build a House for worshipping Him alone.
Stone by stone, they raised its walls.
As they worked, they prayed together: “Our Lord, accept this from us. You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”
keep: The prayer ends with two of Allah’s names side by side, the All-Hearing and the All-Knowing. 32 verses of the Quran end with this same pair.

ibrahim.text:
Allah told Ibrahim to call people to visit the House. “They will come to you on foot and on camels, from every faraway road.”
And they still come, from all over the world, to the House in Makkah that Ibrahim built.
keep: Seven rings of light: pilgrims walk around the House seven times. The camels on the roads are from 22:27.

ibrahim.text:
Say Ibrahim’s prayer
Ibrahim and Isma‘il said it while they built. You can say it when you finish something good.
رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآRabbanā taqabbal minnāOur Lord, accept this from us.

What does the story teach us?
Think for yourself.
Ibrahim looked at the star, the moon and the sun, and asked who made them.

Did you know?
Ibrahim’s name appears 69 times. Only Musa is named more often. Surah 14 is named after him: Surah Ibrahim.
Every verse of the Quran is one tiny square, starting at the top right like a page of the Quran. Each dot is a verse that names Ibrahim.
Allah took Ibrahim as a friend, a khalīl (4:125).

Look closer
Some pictures hide a secret from the Quran itself. Go back and find them.
p. 5–7The star, the moon and the sun. The same three appear again in Yusuf’s dream (12:4). Find them in book 3.p. 10Plates of food in front of the statues. Ibrahim asked them, “Won’t you eat?” (37:91).p. 11Only the biggest statue is left standing (21:58). The axe hanging on it comes from the old commentaries.p. 15Blue flames. Allah said “cool” and then “safe” (21:69). Commentators said “safe” was added so the fire would not become harmfully cold.p. 18The prayer ends with two of Allah’s names side by side, the All-Hearing and the All-Knowing. 32 verses of the Quran end with this same pair.p. 19Seven rings of light: pilgrims walk around the House seven times. The camels on the roads are from 22:27.

For parents
Where the story is told. Al-An‘am 6:74–83 (the star, the moon and the sun), Maryam 19:41–48, Al-Anbiya 21:51–70, As-Saffat 37:83–98 (the statues and the fire), Al-Baqarah 2:124–129 and Al-Hajj 22:26–27 (the House).
Told in simple words. This is a retelling for young children, not a translation. Some details come from the classical commentaries rather than the verses: that the people were away at a festival (37:88–90 points to it), and the axe hung on the largest statue. Many scholars read 6:76–78 as Ibrahim showing his people their error, rather than his own searching; the retelling keeps the words of the verses.
The pictures. By custom, no prophet is drawn, and in this series no person at all. The pictures show the places, the light and the creatures, so your child can picture the story around them.
Talk about it. Ibrahim asked good questions. What is a question you have about Allah, or about the world?
Illustrators welcome. These first pictures are a starting point. Artists are invited to redraw any book; the Books page of the Quran Atlas has a brief for every page.

yusuf.text:
Stories from the Quran · 3
Yusuf and the Eleven Stars
يوسف والكواكب

From the Quran
إِذْ قَالَ يُوسُفُ لِأَبِيهِ يَٰٓأَبَتِ إِنِّى رَأَيْتُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا وَٱلشَّمْسَ وَٱلْقَمَرَ رَأَيْتُهُمْ لِى سَٰجِدِينَ
[Of these stories mention] when Joseph said to his father, "O my father, indeed I have seen [in a dream] eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."
Yusuf 12:4 · Saheeh International

One night a boy named Yusuf (peace be upon him) had a wonderful dream.
“Father,” he said, “I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon. I saw them bowing down to me!”
keep: The same sky: eleven stars, the sun and the moon. The story ends where it began (12:4 and 12:100), like the ring shapes in the Quran Atlas.

yusuf.text:
His father was Prophet Ya‘qub. He understood that Allah had chosen Yusuf for something special.
“My son,” he said gently, “do not tell your brothers about your dream. They may become jealous and plot against you.”

Yusuf had ten older brothers, and they were jealous. “Our father loves Yusuf more than us,” they grumbled.
So they asked their father, “Send Yusuf out with us tomorrow, to run and play.”

But when they were far from home, they threw Yusuf into the bottom of a deep well.
Down in the dark, Allah told Yusuf: “One day you will remind them of what they did, when they do not know who you are.”
keep: The little star in the well is Allah’s promise to Yusuf (12:15).

yusuf.text:
That night the brothers came home crying. They held up Yusuf’s shirt, stained with false blood. “A wolf ate him!”
But Ya‘qub knew they were not telling the truth. “Beautiful patience,” he said. “Allah is the One I ask for help.”
keep: The shirt appears three times: with false blood (12:18), torn from behind (12:25–28), and the shirt that healed (12:93).
The wolf-shaped cloud. The wolf is named three times, all in this surah (12:13, 14, 17), and it never did anything at all.
“Beautiful patience”: Ya‘qub says it twice, in 12:18 and again in 12:83.

yusuf.text:
Then a caravan of travellers came by and stopped at the well. One of them let down his bucket, and up came… a boy!
“Good news!” he called. “Look what I found!”
The travellers sold Yusuf for a few silver coins, and carried him far away, all the way to Egypt.

In Egypt, an important man bought him. “Look after him well,” he told his wife. “He may be useful to us, or we could adopt him as our son.”
Yusuf grew up wise and kind, and Allah gave him knowledge.

When Yusuf was a young man, some people told lies about him. His shirt, torn from behind, showed that he had done nothing wrong.
But still they put him in prison.
keep: The shirt appears three times: with false blood (12:18), torn from behind (12:25–28), and the shirt that healed (12:93).

yusuf.text:
In prison, two men told Yusuf their dreams. One dreamed of pressing grapes. The other dreamed of carrying bread on his head, while birds pecked at it.
Yusuf told them what the dreams meant, and taught them about Allah, the One.

One day the king of Egypt had a strange dream: seven fat cows were eaten by seven thin cows. And there were seven green ears of wheat, and seven dry ones.
No one could explain it, until someone remembered Yusuf.
keep: Count them: seven fat cows, seven thin cows, seven green ears and seven dry ones (12:43).

yusuf.text: “For seven years,” said Yusuf, “plant and harvest. Keep the grain in its ears, except a little to eat. Then seven hard years will come, and you will eat what you saved.”

The king set Yusuf free. “Put me in charge of the storehouses,” said Yusuf. “I will guard them well.”
And he did.

The hard years came, and people travelled from far away to buy grain. One day ten brothers arrived from Yusuf’s homeland.
Yusuf knew them at once. They did not know him at all.

At last he told them: “I am Yusuf!”
His brothers were ashamed and afraid. But Yusuf said: “No blame on you today. May Allah forgive you. He is the most merciful of all.”
keep: “Beautiful patience”: Ya‘qub says it twice, in 12:18 and again in 12:83.

yusuf.text:
Old Ya‘qub had cried so much for Yusuf that he could no longer see. “Take my shirt,” said Yusuf, “and lay it over my father’s face.”
When they did, Ya‘qub could see again!
keep: The shirt appears three times: with false blood (12:18), torn from behind (12:25–28), and the shirt that healed (12:93).

yusuf.text:
The whole family came to Egypt. Yusuf welcomed his parents, and all eleven brothers bowed down before him.
“Father,” said Yusuf, “this is the meaning of my dream from long ago. My Lord has made it come true.”
keep: The same sky: eleven stars, the sun and the moon. The story ends where it began (12:4 and 12:100), like the ring shapes in the Quran Atlas.

yusuf.text:
Words to remember
Two short sayings from Surah Yusuf. One is for waiting. One is for forgiving.
فَصَبْرٌ جَمِيلٌFa-ṣabrun jamīlSo, beautiful patience.

What does the story teach us?
Be patient.
Ya‘qub waited many years, with beautiful patience.

Did you know?
Yusuf’s name appears 27 times, and 25 of them are in one surah. See how the dots crowd together!
Every verse of the Quran is one tiny square, starting at the top right like a page of the Quran. Each dot is a verse that names Yusuf.
Surah Yusuf, number 12, tells his whole story from beginning to end in 111 verses. The Quran calls it “the best of stories” (12:3).

Look closer
Some pictures hide a secret from the Quran itself. Go back and find them.
p. 3, 19The same sky: eleven stars, the sun and the moon. The story ends where it began (12:4 and 12:100), like the ring shapes in the Quran Atlas.p. 7, 11, 18The shirt appears three times: with false blood (12:18), torn from behind (12:25–28), and the shirt that healed (12:93).p. 7The wolf-shaped cloud. The wolf is named three times, all in this surah (12:13, 14, 17), and it never did anything at all.p. 7, 17“Beautiful patience”: Ya‘qub says it twice, in 12:18 and again in 12:83.p. 13Count them: seven fat cows, seven thin cows, seven green ears and seven dry ones (12:43).p. 6The little star in the well is Allah’s promise to Yusuf (12:15).

For parents
Where the story is told. Surah Yusuf 12:4–101. Almost the whole surah is this one story.
Told in simple words. This is a retelling for young children, not a translation. The episode with the wife of the Egyptian official (12:23–34) is told only as “some people told lies about him”; you can tell it more fully when your child is older. The number of coins (12:20 says only “a few”) is left uncounted.
The pictures. By custom, no prophet is drawn, and in this series no person at all. The pictures show the places, the light and the creatures, so your child can picture the story around them.
Talk about it. The brothers were jealous. What does jealousy feel like, and what helps it go away?
Illustrators welcome. These first pictures are a starting point. Artists are invited to redraw any book; the Books page of the Quran Atlas has a brief for every page.

musa.text:
Stories from the Quran · 4
Musa and the River
موسى والنهر

From the Quran
وَأَوْحَيْنَآ إِلَىٰٓ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰٓ أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ فَإِذَا خِفْتِ عَلَيْهِ فَأَلْقِيهِ فِى ٱلْيَمِّ وَلَا تَخَافِى وَلَا تَحْزَنِىٓ إِنَّا رَآدُّوهُ إِلَيْكِ وَجَاعِلُوهُ مِنَ ٱلْمُرْسَلِينَ
And We inspired to the mother of Moses, "Suckle him; but when you fear for him, cast him into the river and do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, We will return him to you and will make him [one] of the messengers."
Al-Qasas 28:7 · Saheeh International

Long ago in Egypt, beside the great river Nile, there was a cruel king called Pharaoh. He made the Children of Israel work as his slaves.
Pharaoh was afraid of them, and he gave a terrible order against their baby boys.

In one of their homes, a baby boy was born. His name was Musa (peace be upon him).
His mother held him close. She loved him so much, and she was very afraid for him.

Then Allah put a message in her heart:
“Feed your baby. And when you are afraid for him, put him in the river. Do not be afraid, and do not be sad. We will bring him back to you, and We will make him one of Our messengers.”
keep: Allah’s promise had two parts: “We will bring him back to you, and make him a messenger” (28:7). Both came true.

musa.text:
So she laid baby Musa in a wooden chest, closed the lid, and set it gently on the water.
Allah had told the river to carry him, and to leave him on the bank.
keep: The river and the sea. The river that carried baby Musa (28:7) and the sea that later swallowed Pharaoh (28:40) are the same Arabic word: al-yamm.
Eight coloured ribbons on the chest: the eight surahs that tell Musa’s story at length, the eight lines of the Atlas train map.

musa.text: Down the great river floated the little chest, past the reeds and the lotus flowers, past the palm trees and the birds.
“Follow him,” Musa’s mother told his sister. So she walked along the riverbank, watching the chest from far away, so that no one would notice her.

The river carried the chest right to the steps of Pharaoh’s palace. Pharaoh’s family lifted it out of the water and opened it.
Inside was a baby!
Pharaoh’s wife loved the baby at once. “He will be a comfort to my eyes, and to yours,” she said to Pharaoh. “Do not kill him. Maybe he will help us, or we can adopt him as our son.”
keep: Two golden stars. “A comfort to my eyes,” said Pharaoh’s wife (28:9). Allah used the same words for his mother: “so that her eyes would be comforted” (28:13).

musa.text:
Back at home, Musa’s mother’s heart felt empty. She almost told everyone her secret.
But Allah made her heart strong, so that she would trust His promise.
keep: The empty cradle. The Quran says her heart became “empty” (28:10).

musa.text: In the palace, the baby was hungry. They brought nurse after nurse to feed him. But Musa refused every single one!
Then his sister came to the palace. “Shall I show you a family who will feed him and care for him kindly?”
And so Allah brought baby Musa back to his mother, so that her eyes would be comforted, and she would not be sad, and she would know that Allah’s promise is true.
keep: Two golden stars. “A comfort to my eyes,” said Pharaoh’s wife (28:9). Allah used the same words for his mother: “so that her eyes would be comforted” (28:13).

musa.text: Musa grew up in Pharaoh’s palace. He became strong, and Allah gave him wisdom and knowledge.

Many years later, far away in a quiet valley, Musa saw a fire on the mountainside. When he came close, Allah spoke to him.
“O Musa, I am Allah, Lord of all the worlds.” Allah made him a messenger.

Allah sent Musa back to Egypt, to Pharaoh, with wonderful signs: his staff and a hand that shone with light.
“Let the Children of Israel go with us,” said Musa. But Pharaoh would not listen.
When Musa led his people out of Egypt, they came to the sea. Allah told Musa to strike it with his staff, and the sea split in two, like two great mountains, with a dry path between.
keep: The river and the sea. The river that carried baby Musa (28:7) and the sea that later swallowed Pharaoh (28:40) are the same Arabic word: al-yamm.

musa.text:
The baby in the chest had become a messenger of Allah, just as Allah had promised his mother on that frightened night.
Allah always keeps His promise.
keep: Allah’s promise had two parts: “We will bring him back to you, and make him a messenger” (28:7). Both came true.

musa.text:
Say Musa’s prayer
Musa prayed this when Allah sent him to Pharaoh. You can say it before something hard, like a test or a new school.
رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِىRabbish-raḥ lī ṣadrīMy Lord, open my heart for me,

What does the story teach us?
Allah keeps His promises.
He promised to bring Musa back to his mother, and He did.

Did you know?
Musa’s name appears 136 times, more than any other person in the Quran. Look how the dots are spread right through the book!
Every verse of the Quran is one tiny square, starting at the top right like a page of the Quran. Each dot is a verse that names Musa.
His story is never told all in one place. Eight surahs tell many parts of it, and the Quran Atlas draws them as a train map, one coloured line for each.

Look closer
Some pictures hide a secret from the Quran itself. Go back and find them.
p. 6, 18The river and the sea. The river that carried baby Musa (28:7) and the sea that later swallowed Pharaoh (28:40) are the same Arabic word: al-yamm.p. 6Eight coloured ribbons on the chest: the eight surahs that tell Musa’s story at length, the eight lines of the Atlas train map.p. 10, 14Two golden stars. “A comfort to my eyes,” said Pharaoh’s wife (28:9). Allah used the same words for his mother: “so that her eyes would be comforted” (28:13).p. 5, 19Allah’s promise had two parts: “We will bring him back to you, and make him a messenger” (28:7). Both came true.p. 11The empty cradle. The Quran says her heart became “empty” (28:10).

For parents
Where the story is told. Al-Qasas 28:3–14 (the birth, the river, the palace and the return), Ta-Ha 20:37–40 (the chest), Al-Qasas 28:29–32 (the fire in the valley and the signs), Ash-Shu‘ara 26:60–66 (the sea).
Told in simple words. This is a retelling for young children, not a translation. Pharaoh’s order against the baby boys (28:4) is mentioned only gently. The last four story pages leap ahead many years to show how the promise of 28:7 was kept; the full story of Musa fills many surahs.
The pictures. By custom, no prophet is drawn, and in this series no person at all. The pictures show the places, the light and the creatures, so your child can picture the story around them.
Talk about it. Musa’s mother was very brave. When have you had to be brave? What helped?
Illustrators welcome. These first pictures are a starting point. Artists are invited to redraw any book; the Books page of the Quran Atlas has a brief for every page.

sulayman.text:
Stories from the Quran · 5
Sulayman and the Ant
سليمان والنملة

From the Quran
حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَآ أَتَوْا۟ عَلَىٰ وَادِ ٱلنَّمْلِ قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّمْلُ ٱدْخُلُوا۟ مَسَٰكِنَكُمْ لَا يَحْطِمَنَّكُمْ سُلَيْمَٰنُ وَجُنُودُهُۥ وَهُمْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ
Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings that you not be crushed by Solomon and his soldiers while they perceive not."
An-Naml 27:18 · Saheeh International

Long ago there lived a wise king and prophet named Dawud, and his son Sulayman (peace be upon him).
Allah gave them both knowledge. Sulayman said, “People, we have been taught the speech of the birds!”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text: Allah gave Sulayman a great kingdom. The wind obeyed him, carrying him a month’s journey in a morning. The jinn worked for him, building palaces, tall arches and great bowls as big as ponds.
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text:
One day Sulayman gathered his army: jinn, people and birds, all in long, neat rows.
Off they marched across the land.
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text: They came to a valley full of ants, thousands and thousands of them, busy carrying seeds and crumbs.
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text:
One ant saw the army coming and called out:
“O ants, go into your homes, so that Sulayman and his soldiers do not crush you without noticing!”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text:
Sulayman heard the tiny ant. He smiled, and laughed at her words, and he stopped his whole army so the ants could get home safely.
Then he prayed: “My Lord, help me to be grateful for all Your blessings.”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text: Later Sulayman looked over the birds. “Why do I not see the hoopoe?” he asked. “Is he missing? If he has no good reason, he will be in trouble!”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?
The empty place in the line of birds. “Why do I not see the hoopoe?” (27:20).

sulayman.text: Soon the hoopoe came flying back. “I have news you do not know!” he said. “I have come from the land of Saba’ with news that is certain.”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text: “There is a queen ruling there, with everything she could wish for, and a magnificent throne. But she and her people bow down to the sun instead of to Allah.”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text:
“We shall see if you are telling the truth,” said Sulayman. He wrote a letter and gave it to the hoopoe to carry.
It began: “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

The letter’s seal. “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful” begins every surah but one. Here it appears in the middle of a surah, the only time (27:30). Count them all, and there are 114: one for each surah.

sulayman.text: The queen read the letter and asked her chiefs what to do. Then she decided to send Sulayman a gift of treasure, to see what he would do.
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text: But Sulayman said: “Are you giving me money? What Allah has given me is better than anything you could give.”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text:
Before the queen arrived, Sulayman asked who could bring her throne to him. One who had knowledge from the Book brought it, in the blink of an eye!
“This is from the kindness of my Lord,” said Sulayman, “to test whether I am grateful.”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?
The sparkles: the throne arrived “before your eye blinks” (27:40).

sulayman.text: When the queen came, she was asked to enter the palace. The floor looked like a pool of water, so she lifted her dress so it would not get wet. But it was smooth glass, with water underneath!
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?
Fish under the floor. The palace floor was “smooth glass” over water (27:44).

sulayman.text: The queen understood. “My Lord,” she said, “I have wronged myself. Now I submit, with Sulayman, to Allah, the Lord of all the worlds.”
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text:
Sulayman was a great king with a great army. Yet he listened to a tiny ant, and he thanked Allah for everything.
To Allah, even the smallest creature matters.
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text: And in the quiet valley, the ants are still busy, carrying their seeds home under the stars.
keep: A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?

sulayman.text:
Say Sulayman’s prayer
Sulayman said it when he heard the ant. You can say it to thank Allah for something good.
رَبِّ أَوْزِعْنِىٓ أَنْ أَشْكُرَ نِعْمَتَكَRabbi awzi‘nī an ashkura ni‘matakMy Lord, help me to be grateful for Your blessing

What does the story teach us?
Say thank you to Allah.
Sulayman had so much, and he was grateful for all of it.

Did you know?
Sulayman’s name appears 17 times in the Quran.
Every verse of the Quran is one tiny square, starting at the top right like a page of the Quran. Each dot is a verse that names Sulayman.
The word for ant, naml, is in just one verse of the whole Quran (27:18), the verse where the ant speaks. And the surah is named after her: Surah An-Naml, The Ant, number 27. The hoopoe is named only once too (27:20).

Look closer
Some pictures hide a secret from the Quran itself. Go back and find them.
p. 3–19A tiny ant hides on every story page. Can you find them all?p. 9The empty place in the line of birds. “Why do I not see the hoopoe?” (27:20).p. 12The letter’s seal. “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful” begins every surah but one. Here it appears in the middle of a surah, the only time (27:30). Count them all, and there are 114: one for each surah.p. 15The sparkles: the throne arrived “before your eye blinks” (27:40).p. 16Fish under the floor. The palace floor was “smooth glass” over water (27:44).

For parents
Where the story is told. An-Naml 27:15–44, with Saba’ 34:12–15 and Al-Anbiya 21:78–82 for the wind, the jinn and Saba’.
Told in simple words. This is a retelling for young children, not a translation. The queen is not named in the Quran; tradition calls her Bilqis. The one who brought the throne is described only as “one who had knowledge from the Book” (27:40). The hidden ants are the editor’s game, not part of the verses.
The pictures. By custom, no prophet is drawn, and in this series no person at all. The pictures show the places, the light and the creatures, so your child can picture the story around them.
Talk about it. Sulayman listened to the smallest creature. Who is someone small or quiet that we should listen to more?
Illustrators welcome. These first pictures are a starting point. Artists are invited to redraw any book; the Books page of the Quran Atlas has a brief for every page.

yunus.text:
Stories from the Quran · 6
Yunus and the Big Fish
يونس والحوت
keep: Four golden stars on the whale: Yunus is named four times in the Quran.

yunus.text:
From the Quran
فَٱسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُۥ وَنَجَّيْنَٰهُ مِنَ ٱلْغَمِّ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نُۨجِى ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ
So We responded to him and saved him from the distress. And thus do We save the believers.
Al-Anbiyaʾ 21:88 · Saheeh International

Long, long ago, there was a great city beside a river, full of busy streets and markets. More than a hundred thousand people lived there.
Allah sent a prophet to them. His name was Yunus (peace be upon him).

“Worship Allah alone,” Yunus told the people, “and do what is good.” He called them again and again, day after day.
But they shut their doors and would not listen.

Yunus grew angry and upset with his people, and he left the city.
But he did not wait for Allah to tell him to go. That was his mistake.

He walked all the way to the sea. A ship was in the harbour, full of people and piled high with heavy loads.
Yunus climbed aboard, and the ship sailed out across the wide blue sea.
keep: The ship. The Quran calls it “the laden ship” (37:140), the very same words used for Nuh’s ark (26:119). Find the ark in book 1.

yunus.text: Far from land, the wind began to roar. Great waves crashed over the ship. It was too full, and it was in danger of sinking!

The sailors drew lots to choose who must leave the ship to make it lighter.
Three times they drew, and three times the lot fell on Yunus.
keep: The bowl with a dot above it is shaped like the Arabic letter ن, nūn. Nūn also means fish, which is why Yunus is called Dhun-Nun. And the surah that calls him “the one of the fish” (68:48) begins with the letter ن.

yunus.text: So Yunus went down into the stormy sea. And from far below, Allah sent a huge fish…

…and the fish swallowed Yunus whole. It did not bite him or hurt him. It simply carried him down, down into the deep.
GULP!

Inside the fish it was dark.
Dark inside the fish. Dark in the deep sea. Dark in the night. Three darknesses, one inside another.
keep: Three gold stars for the three darknesses: the night, the sea and the fish.

yunus.text:
In the darkness, Yunus remembered Allah. He knew he had done wrong, and he called out:
لَّآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنتَ سُبْحَٰنَكَ إِنِّى كُنتُ مِنَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
Lā ilāha illā anta, subḥānaka, innī kuntu minaẓ-ẓālimīn.
“There is no god but You. Glory be to You! I have done wrong.”

Allah heard him.
The Quran says that if Yunus had not been one of those who remember and praise Allah, he would have stayed inside the fish until the Last Day. But he did remember, and Allah saved him from his sorrow.
The great fish swam up from the deep, all the way to the shore, and there it put Yunus out onto the sand.
The shore was bare, with no trees and no shade at all. The sun beat down, and Yunus was weak and ill.
Then Allah made a plant grow up over him, a gourd vine, growing and growing, curling and climbing…
…until its big, wide leaves made a cool green shade. There Yunus rested and ate, until he was well and strong again.
keep: One golden gourd. The word for this plant, yaqṭīn, appears only once in the whole Quran (37:146).

yunus.text: Then Allah sent Yunus back to his people. While he had been away, they had seen signs of Allah’s punishment coming, and they had turned to Allah.

And this time, they believed, more than a hundred thousand of them! Allah took the punishment away, and they lived in peace for a long time.
They are the only town in the Quran that believed just in time.

Say Yunus’s prayer
One piece at a time. You can say it whenever you feel scared or sad, or when you have done something wrong.
لَّآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنتَLā ilāha illā antaThere is no god but You.

What does the story teach us?
Be patient.
Wait for Allah’s plan, even when things are hard.

Did you know?
Yunus’s name is in just 4 verses of the Quran. Can you find the 4 golden dots? They are 4:163, 6:86, 10:98, 37:139.
Every verse of the Quran is one tiny square, starting at the top right like a page of the Quran. Each dot is a verse that names Yunus.
He has another name too: Dhun-Nun, “the one of the fish” (21:87). And a whole surah is named after him: Surah Yunus, number 10.

Look closer
Some pictures hide a secret from the Quran itself. Go back and find them.
p. 1Four golden stars on the whale: Yunus is named four times in the Quran.p. 6The ship. The Quran calls it “the laden ship” (37:140), the very same words used for Nuh’s ark (26:119). Find the ark in book 1.p. 8The bowl with a dot above it is shaped like the Arabic letter ن, nūn. Nūn also means fish, which is why Yunus is called Dhun-Nun. And the surah that calls him “the one of the fish” (68:48) begins with the letter ن.p. 11Three gold stars for the three darknesses: the night, the sea and the fish.p. 17One golden gourd. The word for this plant, yaqṭīn, appears only once in the whole Quran (37:146).

For parents
Where the story is told. As-Saffat 37:139–148 (the ship, the lots, the fish, the shore, the gourd plant, the hundred thousand); Al-Anbiya 21:87–88 (his prayer in the darknesses); Al-Qalam 68:48–50; Yunus 10:98 (his people believed and were spared).
Told in simple words. This is a retelling for young children, not a translation. Some details come from the classical commentaries, such as Ibn Kathir’s, rather than the Quran’s own words: the storm, the lots drawn three times, the three darknesses, and that his people saw signs of punishment before believing. The city is not named in the Quran; tradition names it Nineveh.
The prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said that no Muslim prays with the prayer of Dhun-Nun for anything without Allah answering him (Tirmidhi 3505).
The pictures. By custom, no prophet is drawn, and in this series no person at all. The pictures show the places, the light and the creatures, so your child can picture the story around them.
Talk about it. Yunus left before Allah told him to, then said sorry in the dark. When did you last say sorry? What helps when you feel alone?
Illustrators welcome. These first pictures are a starting point. Artists are invited to redraw any book; the Books page of the Quran Atlas has a brief for every page.

maryam.text:
Stories from the Quran · 7
Maryam and the Date Palm
مريم والنخلة

From the Quran
وَهُزِّىٓ إِلَيْكِ بِجِذْعِ ٱلنَّخْلَةِ تُسَٰقِطْ عَلَيْكِ رُطَبًا جَنِيًّا
And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates.
Maryam 19:25 · Saheeh International
Long ago, a woman from the family of ‘Imran was expecting a baby. She prayed: “My Lord, I give the child I am carrying to You, to serve You. Please accept it from me.”

Her baby was a girl. “I have named her Maryam,” said her mother, “and I ask You to protect her and her children.”
And Allah accepted Maryam with a beautiful acceptance.
Prophet Zakariyya looked after Maryam. She spent her days in a quiet prayer room, worshipping Allah. Every time Zakariyya came in, he found fresh food beside her.
keep: Snow at the window, and summer fruit in the bowl. The commentators said Zakariyya found fruit out of season (3:37).

maryam.text:
“Maryam,” he asked, “where does this come from?”
“It is from Allah,” she said. “Allah gives to whoever He wills, more than can be counted.”

Maryam grew up good and pure, and Allah chose her above all the women of the world.
One day she went to a quiet place to the east, and hung a curtain to be alone.
Allah sent an angel to her. “I am a messenger from your Lord,” he said, “to give you a pure baby boy.”

“How can I have a son?” asked Maryam. “No man has married me.”
“It is easy for Allah,” said the angel. “He only says ‘Be!’, and it is. Your son will be a sign for people, and a mercy from Allah.”
When the time came near, Maryam went away to a place far from everyone.
She came to the trunk of a date palm. She was tired and in pain, and very worried about what people would say.
Then a voice called to her from below: “Do not be sad! Your Lord has made a little stream flow beneath you.”
keep: The little stream. The Quran’s word is sariyy (19:24).

maryam.text: “Shake the trunk of the palm tree towards you, and fresh, ripe dates will fall down for you.”
keep: Fresh, ripe dates. The word for them, ruṭab, is used only once in the whole Quran (19:25).

maryam.text:
“So eat, and drink, and be happy.”
And Maryam’s baby was born: a boy named ‘Isa (peace be upon him).
Maryam came back to her people, carrying her baby. Allah had told her: “If you see anyone, do not speak today.”

“Maryam!” the people cried. “You have done something strange!”
Maryam did not answer. She simply pointed to the baby.
“How can we talk to a baby in a cradle?” they said.

Then baby ‘Isa spoke!
“I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Book, and made me a prophet. He has made me kind to my mother.”

“Peace be on me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised to life again.”
Everyone had heard a newborn baby speak.
keep: Three stars: the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised (19:33).

maryam.text:
‘Isa grew up to be a great prophet. By Allah’s permission, he shaped birds from clay, breathed into them, and they flew away as real birds!
And his mother Maryam is remembered by name in the Quran forever.
keep: Birds of clay. In 5:110, Allah says “by My permission” four times in a single verse, for each of ‘Isa’s miracles.

maryam.text:
Say Maryam’s words
Maryam said this when Zakariyya asked where her food came from. You can say it about every good thing you have.
هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِHuwa min ‘indillāhIt is from Allah.

What does the story teach us?
Everything good is from Allah.
“It is from Allah,” said Maryam.

Did you know?
Maryam is the only woman called by her name in the Quran, and Surah Maryam, number 19, is named after her. Her son ‘Isa is named 25 times.
Every verse of the Quran is one tiny square, starting at the top right like a page of the Quran. Each dot is a verse that names ‘Isa.
The Quran compares ‘Isa to Adam: Allah made both by saying “Be!” (3:59). Counted by name, Adam is also named exactly 25 times.

Look closer
Some pictures hide a secret from the Quran itself. Go back and find them.
p. 5Snow at the window, and summer fruit in the bowl. The commentators said Zakariyya found fruit out of season (3:37).p. 12The little stream. The Quran’s word is sariyy (19:24).p. 13Fresh, ripe dates. The word for them, ruṭab, is used only once in the whole Quran (19:25).p. 18Three stars: the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised (19:33).p. 19Birds of clay. In 5:110, Allah says “by My permission” four times in a single verse, for each of ‘Isa’s miracles.

For parents
Where the story is told. Al ‘Imran 3:35–37 and 3:42–49, Maryam 19:16–34, and Al-Ma’idah 5:110.
Told in simple words. This is a retelling for young children, not a translation. The angel (19:17, “Our spirit”, understood as Jibril) is shown only as light. How ‘Isa came to be is told as the verses tell it: “It is easy for Allah.” The fruit out of season comes from the commentaries. The place of the birth is not named in the Quran.
The pictures. By custom, no prophet is drawn, and in this series no person at all. The pictures show the places, the light and the creatures, so your child can picture the story around them.
Talk about it. Maryam was worried about what people would say. What do you do when you are worried?

cave.text:
Stories from the Quran · 8
The Sleepers in the Cave
أصحاب الكهف

From the Quran
نَّحْنُ نَقُصُّ عَلَيْكَ نَبَأَهُم بِٱلْحَقِّ إِنَّهُمْ فِتْيَةٌ ءَامَنُوا۟ بِرَبِّهِمْ وَزِدْنَٰهُمْ هُدًى
It is We who relate to you, [O Muhammad], their story in truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.
Al-Kahf 18:13 · Saheeh International

Long ago there was a city where the people worshipped idols, and the king was hard on anyone who did not.
But a few young men in that city believed in Allah, the One. And Allah made their faith stronger.
They stood up bravely and said: “Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never call on any god but Him.”
To keep their faith safe, they left the city and climbed into the mountains to a cave. And their dog came along too.

At the mouth of the cave, they prayed:
“Our Lord, give us mercy from You, and guide us to what is right.”
Then Allah made them fall asleep, a deep, deep sleep, right there in the cave.
Each morning the rising sun leaned away from their cave to the right. Each evening the setting sun passed them by on the left. They lay safe in the cool shade inside.
keep: The sun’s path. Rising, it leans away to the right; setting, it passes them on the left (18:17).

cave.text: If you had looked in, you would have thought they were awake, but they were fast asleep. Allah turned them over, to the right and to the left.
And their dog lay at the doorway, his front paws stretched out, keeping watch.
keep: The dog’s front paws stretched out at the doorway, exactly as 18:18 describes.

cave.text: They slept and slept. They slept for three hundred years, and nine more.
keep: 309 little moons: “three hundred years, and they added nine” (18:25). Commentators noted that 300 years by the sun are about 309 years by the moon.

cave.text:
Then Allah woke them up. They yawned and stretched. “How long have we been here?” one asked.
“A day,” said another, “or part of a day.”
“Allah knows best how long,” they agreed.
“We are hungry,” they said. “Let one of us take these silver coins to the city and buy the purest food. But be careful, and let no one notice you!”
keep: Silver coins. The Quran’s word is wariq, silver money (18:19).

cave.text: But the city had changed completely! New streets, new buildings, new people. And the old coin was from a time hundreds of years before.
Now the people of the city believed in Allah. The sleepers were a sign for them: Allah’s promise is true, and He can bring people back to life.

Later, people argued: “There were three, and the fourth was their dog.” “No, five, and the sixth was their dog!” “Seven, and the eighth was their dog!”
The Quran says: “My Lord knows best how many they were.”
keep: In 18:22 the first two guesses are called “guessing at the unseen”; the third is not. Ibn ‘Abbas said he was one of the few who know: seven, and their dog.

cave.text: Allah also taught: Never say “I will do it tomorrow” without adding “if Allah wills”: in shā’ Allāh. Only Allah knows what tomorrow will bring.
“Do you think the people of the cave were a wonder?” Allah asks. All of His signs are wonders: the stars, the sun, and every new morning.
And whenever you read Surah Al-Kahf, The Cave, you can remember the brave young men who trusted Allah, and their faithful dog.

Say the sleepers’ prayer
They prayed it at the mouth of the cave. You can say it whenever you need help to do the right thing.
رَبَّنَآ ءَاتِنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةًRabbanā ātinā min ladunka raḥmatanOur Lord, give us mercy from You,

What does the story teach us?
Stand up for what is right.
The young men said “Our Lord is Allah,” even when it was hard.

Did you know?
Surah Al-Kahf is number 18, and their story is told in exactly 18 verses of it, from 18:9 to 18:26. Can you find the dots?
Every verse of the Quran is one tiny square, starting at the top right like a page of the Quran. Each dot is one verse of the sleepers’ story.
Many Muslims read Surah Al-Kahf every Friday. The dog is mentioned four times, all in 18:18 and 18:22.

Look closer
Some pictures hide a secret from the Quran itself. Go back and find them.
p. 8The sun’s path. Rising, it leans away to the right; setting, it passes them on the left (18:17).p. 10The dog’s front paws stretched out at the doorway, exactly as 18:18 describes.p. 11309 little moons: “three hundred years, and they added nine” (18:25). Commentators noted that 300 years by the sun are about 309 years by the moon.p. 13Silver coins. The Quran’s word is wariq, silver money (18:19).p. 16In 18:22 the first two guesses are called “guessing at the unseen”; the third is not. Ibn ‘Abbas said he was one of the few who know: seven, and their dog.

For parents
Where the story is told. Al-Kahf 18:9–26.
Told in simple words. This is a retelling for young children, not a translation. The king’s cruelty and the changed city come from the commentaries; the verses say only that their people worshipped other gods (18:15) and that the sleepers feared being stoned or forced back (18:20). The Quran does not give the city’s name or the young men’s names.
The pictures. By custom, no prophet is drawn, and in this series no person at all. The pictures show the places, the light and the creatures, so your child can picture the story around them.
Talk about it. The young men were brave together. Who helps you be brave?
Illustrators welcome. These first pictures are a starting point. Artists are invited to redraw any book; the Books page of the Quran Atlas has a brief for every page.
